summary:
Pulse Health is a self-contained health intelligence web app that runs fully onboard, without a ground connection, and helps astronauts assess their own health and act on it during long-duration missions. As human spaceflight evolves toward extended expeditions where communication delays and blackouts limit real-time consultations with Earth-based flight surgeons, crews must be able to detect, interpret, and manage medical risks independently.

Designed around NASA’s five spaceflight hazards, the app unifies continuous wearable telemetry, guided onboard exams and diagnostics, check-in reminders, and an interactive 3D anatomical atlas. Rather than displaying raw numbers in isolation, an onboard triage engine compares each reading with the crew member’s history and baseline and translates subtle physiological shifts into preventive countermeasures and clear next steps. This gives crews the clinical autonomy that missions beyond low Earth orbit will require.
details:
What it does

Spaceflight slowly changes the human body. Fluids shift toward the head, circadian rhythms break down, metabolism drifts, and radiation and isolation take their toll. Pulse Health brings decades of NASA research into an onboard app that helps crew members notice these changes early and decide what to do next without waiting for the ground.

How it works

The app follows six indicators: heart rate, blood glucose, sleep, blood pressure, core temperature, and readiness and mood. Each reading is compared with the crew member’s own history and baseline. The result is one of five states (Normal, Observation, Attention, Critical or No data), and it comes with the reason behind it, when to measure again and when to escalate. A missing or invalid reading is reported as missing, so a sensor failure never looks like good health.

Exam reminders explain how to perform each test, such as a fasting glucose check, and a logged result is classified right away for its context: fasting, after a meal or after exercise. A daily check-in takes about fifteen seconds. In it, the astronaut records mood, stress and sleep recovery, and the readiness score updates to catch fatigue before it builds up.

Radiation is tracked as a hazard of its own. Solar particle events from NASA DONKI and dose rates measured by the RAD instrument on the Curiosity rover feed an accumulated dose budget, compared against the career limit in NASA-STD-3001. When a vital sign drifts or an urgent event occurs, the alert panel shows what needs attention and opens the matching emergency protocol, step by step, in one click. A 3D model from the Human Reference Atlas lets the crew explore the organs and systems their data refers to, and a sensors page shows whether each wearable is reporting reliable data.

Benefits and intended impact

On missions to the Moon and Mars, a message to Earth and back can take up to 40 minutes, and blackouts can last much longer. Pulse Health is meant to give crews enough information to understand their own condition and act on it in that gap. We expect earlier detection, fewer situations that turn into emergencies, and more autonomy for crews beyond low Earth orbit

Tools and technologies

  • React 19, TypeScript, Vite and React Router
  • Three.js for the 3D atlas, Recharts for charts and Lucide for icons
  • Vitest and Testing Library (126 automated tests), and ESLint
  • Python and Jupyter (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn) for the research notebooks
  • NASA data from NTRS (41,866 life sciences documents), the OSDR Biological Data API, the NASA Life Sciences Portal, DONKI and MSL RAD on the Planetary Data System

We used no physical hardware. The wearable telemetry is simulated through demo scenarios, such as hypoglycemia, sleep debt or a gap in the data, so anyone can see how the app reacts to each situation.

What makes it creative

Most health dashboards stop at the number. We wanted each indicator to say what is happening, why it matters in space and what to do now. We also show the space environment next to the body, because radiation and solar activity change how a vital sign should be read.

Factors we considered

Several decisions came from the conditions of a long mission. The app works with no ground connection, because the crew cannot count on one. Check-ins are short and actions take one click, because crew time is scarce. The app supports decisions but does not diagnose: when data is missing or unreliable, it says so and escalates conservatively. Indicators and thresholds come from NASA research and the Human Research Program Evidence Reports, which we explored in our notebooks. The interface supports screen readers, light and dark themes, and both English and Portuguese.
